claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially has a high-temperature BCC state.
Rapid cooling traps local compositional fluctuations in the high-temperature BCC phase.
Rapidly cooled Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 contains transient microsegregation within its BCC matrix.
Cooling-induced compositional inhomogeneities act as preferential nucleation sites for secondary phases during subsequent thermal exposure.
Cooling rate can affect phase stability and transformation behavior in multicomponent alloys.
Slower cooling brings an alloy closer to equilibrium conditions.
Slow cooling of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 permits more uniform elemental redistribution and compositional homogenization.
Greater compositional homogeneity after slow cooling reduces secondary-phase nucleation during aging.
The proposed effect is important under non-equilibrium cooling conditions where diffusion is limited.
Microsegregation trapped by quenching remains kinetically active during intermediate aging near 750 °C.
Long or sufficiently high-temperature aging can erase the initial microsegregation through diffusion.
Rapidly quenched samples will develop a higher density of secondary phases during identical isothermal aging than slowly cooled samples.
Rapidly quenched samples will develop a finer dispersion of secondary phases during identical isothermal aging than slowly cooled samples.
Different cooling histories can produce distinct DSC transformation signatures or shifted transformation temperatures.
Additional or shifted DSC and XRD features in the target alloy will correlate with the extent of microsegregation.
The rapid-quench and slow-cooling groups should receive the same subsequent isothermal aging treatment.
Failure to observe a statistically significant cooling-history-dependent difference in secondary-phase density, dispersion, or transformation behavior would falsify the proposed causal hypothesis.
